projects.title: PersonaPlex Full-Duplex STS
projects.desc: Experiment: Testing NVIDIA's PersonaPlex-7B full-duplex Speech-to-Speech model with ~170ms latency and native turn-taking.
projects.fullContent:
Note: This is an experiment to test and explore NVIDIA's PersonaPlex model. All model development and research credit goes to NVIDIA and Kyutai (Moshi architecture). I set up this environment to understand and evaluate the capabilities of full-duplex Speech-to-Speech systems.

PersonaPlex is NVIDIA's breakthrough real-time, full-duplex Speech-to-Speech conversational AI platform. Unlike traditional voice assistants that wait for you to finish speaking, PersonaPlex can listen and respond simultaneously, just like a real human conversation.

Why This Experiment?

I wanted to understand how modern Speech-to-Speech (STS) models work without the traditional ASR -> LLM -> TTS pipeline. PersonaPlex processes audio directly, which enables ultra-low latency and natural turn-taking.

Key Features (NVIDIA)

FeatureDescription
Ultra-Low Latency~170ms response time for real-time conversations
Full-DuplexModel listens while speaking and handles interruptions naturally
18 Voice OptionsNatural (NATF/NATM) and Variety (VARF/VARM) voices
Dynamic PersonasText-based role prompts following NVIDIA's format
Voice PreviewsPre-generated samples for each voice option

Architecture Overview

+------------+    +------------+    +------------+
|  Frontend  |<-->|  Backend   |<-->| PersonaPlex|
| (React/TS) |WSS | (FastAPI)  |    |  -7B Model |
+------------+    +------------+    +------------+

Neural Audio Codec: Mimi

  • Compresses 24kHz audio into discrete tokens at 12.5 Hz
  • Uses 8 parallel codebooks for high-fidelity reconstruction
  • Enables direct audio-to-audio processing without text intermediary

Language Model: PersonaPlex-7B

  • Full-duplex conversational model (listens while speaking)
  • Trained on synthetic conversations + Fisher corpus
  • Supports voice prompts (timbre) and text prompts (persona)

My Setup

ComponentTechnology
FrontendReact, TypeScript, WebSocket (WSS)
BackendFastAPI, Python, SSL/HTTPS
ModelNVIDIA PersonaPlex-7B (HuggingFace)
RequirementsNVIDIA GPU with 16GB+ VRAM, Python 3.10+

References

  • NVIDIA PersonaPlex Paper
  • PersonaPlex-7B on HuggingFace
  • NVIDIA PersonaPlex GitHub

projects.title: MineStream Voice Synthesis
projects.desc: Experiment: Local-first AI voice synthesis with Qwen3-TTS dual-model architecture for voice cloning and prompt-based generation.
projects.fullContent:
MineStream is a local-first AI voice generation tool I built to experiment with Qwen3-TTS's dual-model architecture. It enables high-fidelity text-to-speech with three distinct modes: library voices, prompt-based voice design, and zero-shot voice cloning.

What I Built

The goal was to create a unified interface for exploring different TTS paradigms, from traditional preset voices to cutting-edge voice cloning. The system runs entirely locally, prioritizing privacy and low-latency generation.

System Status

ComponentStatusNotes
Frontend (Vite + React + TS)WorkingToasts, Avatars, Audio Visualizers
Backend (FastAPI + SQLite)WorkingHTTPS enabled for mobile support
Voice CloningActivePowered by Qwen3-Base (Zero-Shot)
Voice Design (Prompts)ActivePowered by Qwen3-VoiceDesign
Audio PipelineOptimizedAuto-converts WebM/MP3 to 24kHz WAV

Three Voice Modes

Library Mode

Use preset voices or previously cloned voices from your personal collection. Quick access to proven voice profiles.

Prompt Mode

Describe any voice in natural language: "A rusty old pirate" or "A cheerful young woman with a British accent" and the model generates it on the fly.

Cloning Mode

Upload any audio sample (3-10 seconds) to clone a voice instantly using zero-shot learning. No fine-tuning required.

Tech Stack

LayerTechnology
FrontendReact, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide
BackendFastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, Pydantic
AI ModelsQwen3-VoiceDesign (Prompts) + Qwen3-Base (Cloning)
Audioffmpeg (pydub), torchaudio, Web Audio API

Dual-Model Architecture

The system uses two specialized Qwen3 models working together:

  • Qwen3-VoiceDesign: Generates voice embeddings from text descriptions. Great for creative voice design without reference audio.
  • Qwen3-Base: Powers zero-shot voice cloning by extracting speaker embeddings from short audio samples.
Note: First run downloads ~7GB of model weights (VoiceDesign + Base). Ensure sufficient disk space.

Key Challenges Solved

  • Audio Format Handling: Backend auto-normalizes WebM/MP3 uploads to 24kHz WAV using ffmpeg
  • Mobile Microphone Access: HTTPS enabled by default for secure mic access on external devices
  • Model Switching: Seamless switching between voice modes without reloading models

projects.title: SpeechRAG with META SONAR
projects.desc: Experiment: Cross-modal RAG using Meta's SONAR for real-time context injection into speech - no STT required.
projects.fullContent:
SpeechRAG Pipeline is a real-time, cross-modal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system I built to experiment with audio-to-text semantic search. The key innovation: it retrieves relevant text using raw audio embeddings, completely bypassing traditional Speech-to-Text (STT).

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Traditional voice assistants follow a pipeline: Audio -> STT -> Text Search -> Response. Each step adds latency and potential errors. What if we could search directly from audio embeddings?

Meta's SONAR (Sentence-level multimOdal and laNguage-Agnostic Representations) model can embed both speech and text into a shared 1024-dimensional vector space. This means spoken queries can directly match against text documents!

Key Features

FeatureDescription
Cross-Modal RAGRetrieves text alerts using raw audio embeddings, no STT required
Real-Time ProcessingDesigned for less than 160ms end-to-end latency
Meta SONAR IntegrationUses sonar_speech_encoder_eng and text_sonar_basic_encoder
Vector SearchQdrant for high-performance similarity search
Neural DashboardReal-time WebSocket frontend to visualize context injections

System Architecture

Three containerized services orchestrated via Docker Compose:

1. SpeechRAG Core

FastAPI and WebSocket server. The LogicBrain orchestrates the RAG flow: Audio -> Vector -> Search -> Threshold -> Injection. Uses AudioStreamBuffer for sliding window processing.

2. SONAR Encoder Service

Dedicated microservice running PyTorch and sonar-space. Exposes HTTP endpoints for encoding Audio (PCM16) and Text into 1024-dim vectors. CUDA GPU accelerated.

3. Vector Database (Qdrant)

Stores semantic embeddings of operational alerts. Enables efficient similarity search with tunable thresholds.

Tech Stack

LayerTechnology
CorePython, FastAPI, WebSocket
MLMeta SONAR, PyTorch, CUDA
InfrastructureDocker Compose, Qdrant
FrontendHTML/JS Neural Dashboard

Calibration and Thresholds

The system uses calibrated similarity thresholds to distinguish relevant context from noise:

ScenarioSimilarity ScoreAction
Valid Query~0.43+Inject Context
Current Threshold0.38Decision Boundary
Noise/Silence~0.26Filter Out

This ensures random conversation or silence does not trigger irrelevant context injections.

Key Learnings

  • Cross-modal embeddings work: SONAR's shared vector space genuinely enables audio-to-text retrieval
  • Threshold tuning is critical: The gap between valid matches (~0.43) and noise (~0.26) required careful calibration
  • Dockerization simplifies ML: Separating the SONAR service made deployment and scaling much cleaner

projects.title: GitFluent
projects.desc: AI-powered CLI tool that translates natural language into precise, executable Git commands.
projects.fullContent:
Gitfluent is an AI-powered CLI tool that translates natural language into precise, executable Git commands.

Built on top of Meta's Llama-3 (8B) and fine-tuned with Unsloth, it bridges the gap between human intent and technical syntax. Whether you're a beginner afraid of git reset or a senior engineer tired of typing complex interactive rebases, Gitfluent has you covered.

Why Gitfluent?

The gap between "I want to undo my last commit" and knowing to type git reset --soft HEAD~1 is a major friction point for developers.

Gitfluent solves this by:

  • Understanding Intent: It knows the difference between "undo" (soft reset) and "delete" (hard reset).
  • Chaining Logic: It can generate multi-step commands (e.g., create a branch -> switch to it -> push upstream) in a single line.
  • Handling Context: It understands complex requests like resolving merge conflicts or cherry-picking specific hashes.

Installation

1. Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/zhnuksyh/gitfluent.git
cd gitfluent

2. Install dependencies

IMPORTANT: Requires a GPU-enabled environment or appropriate CPU libraries for quantization support.
pip install -r requirements.txt

Usage

You can run Gitfluent directly from your terminal using the provided Python wrapper.

Basic Syntax

python gitfluent.py "Your natural language request here"

Examples

GoalNatural Language InputGenerated Command
Undo a mistake"Undo my last commit but keep the files staged"git reset --soft HEAD~1
Complex Branching"Create a new branch named feature-login and switch to it"git checkout -b feature-login
Merge Conflicts"Keep the incoming changes for style.css and ignore my local version"git checkout --theirs style.css && git add style.css

Model Details

  • Architecture: Llama-3 (8B Parameters)
  • Quantization: 4-bit (via bitsandbytes) for efficient local inference.
  • Fine-Tuning Framework: Unsloth (2x faster training, 0% accuracy loss).
  • Dataset: Custom dataset focusing on version control edge cases, conflict resolution, and colloquial technical requests.

Download the Model Weights: The full model weights are hosted on Hugging Face: daimon-ml/gitfluent-llama3-8b

Disclaimer

Gitfluent is a generative AI model. While it is fine-tuned for high accuracy, it can occasionally hallucinate or output incorrect commands.

Always review the command before executing it, especially destructive commands like reset --hard or clean -f. Use at your own risk.

Contributing

Contributions are welcome! If you find a Git command the model struggles with, feel free to open an issue or submit a PR with new training examples.

License

This project is licensed under the Apache 2.0 License.

projects.title: Interact
projects.desc: Interactive educational tool for visualizing various Machine Learning concepts.
projects.fullContent:
ML Interact is an interactive educational tool for visualizing various Machine Learning concepts. This project aims to provide an intuitive and hands-on way to understand the building blocks of modern AI systems.

Live Demo: https://zhnuksyh.github.io/ml-interact/

Features

The application is broken down into several interactive modules, each focusing on a specific concept:

  • Chunking: Visualize how text is split into smaller pieces for processing.
  • Embeddings: Explore how text is converted into vector representations.
  • Vector Search (RAG): Understand Retrieval-Augmented Generation through vector similarity search.
  • Quantization: See the effects of reducing model precision.
  • Full Pipeline: visualize the end-to-end flow of an LLM application.
  • LLM Basics: Learn about the fundamental components of Large Language Models.
  • Inference: Interact with model inference steps.
  • Vision / OCR: Explore Optical Character Recognition and vision capabilities.
  • MCP / Tools: a section for Model Context Protocol and external tools.

Tech Stack

  • Framework: React
  • Build Tool: Vite
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS
  • Icons: Lucide React

Getting Started

To run this project locally, follow these steps:

1. Install dependencies

npm install

2. Start the development server

npm run dev

3. Open in browser

Open your browser and navigate to the URL shown in the terminal (usually http://localhost:5173).

Why This Exists

Most "Free" QR generators are:

  • Paywalled: They blur high-quality downloads unless you upgrade to "Pro".

Static QR Forge is different. It generates standard, static QR codes directly on your computer. The pixel pattern is the URL. It works offline, forever, and for free.

Features

  • 100% Client-Side: No server, no database, no tracking.
  • Vector Quality: Export crystal-clear SVGs or high-res PNGs (2000px+).
  • Customizable: Change colors, shapes, dot styles, and backgrounds.
  • Logo Support: Embed your brand logo seamlessly.
  • Privacy Focused: Secure by design.

Tech Stack

  • React + TypeScript: For robust component logic.
  • Vite: For lightning-fast development and building.
  • Tailwind CSS: For the premium, dark-mode UI.
  • qr-code-styling: The powerful engine behind the generation (loaded dynamically).

articles.title: Is the Cascaded Approach Still the Way to Go for Full-Duplex Voice AI?
articles.desc: Exploring the trade-offs of the STT to LLM to TTS pipeline for real-time conversational AI, from latency challenges to GPU orchestration nightmares.
articles.fullContent:
I've been researching Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech (STS) systems lately, and the complexity is.. fascinating. While the dream is a Jarvis-like assistant, the architectural choices are anything but simple.

Currently, I'm exploring the trade-offs of the Cascaded Model (STT to LLM to TTS). It's the standard workhorse, but as I look closer, the challenges are stacking up:

1. The Latency Tax

In a world where humans expect a response in less than 500ms, a cascade is a race against time. Every millisecond spent in ASR buffering or LLM's first token generation eats into the budget.

2. The Interruption Puzzle

How do you design a system that listens while speaking, without it feeling robotic? I'm looking at VAD (Voice Activity Detection) strategies that can distinguish between a user's "uh-huh" (backchanneling) and a true stop command.

3. The Retrieval Bottleneck (RAG and MCP)

Integrating RAG or the Model Context Protocol (MCP) adds a massive thinking delay. Fetching live data via MCP is great for accuracy, but it often breaks the fluid rhythm of a conversation. How do we balance "being smart" with "being fast" when every extra second of retrieval makes the AI sound like it's stalling?

4. The Infrastructure Nightmare (GPU and PyTorch)

This is the part I notice people rarely talk about. Running three separate state-of-the-art models simultaneously is a VRAM hog. I'm currently wrestling with GPU memory allocation to prevent OOM (Out of Memory) errors, not to mention the "version hell" of incompatible PyTorch dependencies between different STT and TTS libraries.

5. Context Window vs. Performance

As the conversation gets longer, managing the context window becomes a double-edged sword. You need the history for coherence, but larger contexts increase the LLM processing time, pushing us further away from that sub-500ms latency goal.

Looking at Native Multi-Modal Models

I'm currently deep in the research for native multi-modal models like Moshi by Kyutai and Qwen2.5-Omni. Unlike the cascaded mess, these models attempt to handle audio natively, potentially solving the emotion and latency gaps. But moving from cascade to moshi/omni brings a whole new set of research questions regarding steerability and deployment at scale.

Open Questions

I'm still in the thick of this research. If you've worked or are currently working on full-duplex systems, I wonder:

  • How is GPU orchestration handled in production?
  • What's the latency of external tool-calling in your systems?
  • Is the cascade still viable for high-stakes enterprise use?

Would love to hear your thoughts and experiences!

articles.title: How I Shared My First Mobile (Web) Game with Friends (without the App Store)
articles.desc: I finally finished building my first mobile game, Ditto!, but hit a snag with App Store fees. Here is how I used Progressive Web Apps (PWA) to share it for free and give it a native feel.
articles.fullContent:
I finally did it. I finished building my first mobile game, Ditto!. It’s a simple little memory game where you match sequences. Nothing too fancy, but I was proud of it haha.

Naturally, the first thing I wanted to do was text my group chat and say, "Hey guys, download my game!"

But when I looked into actually putting it on the App Store, I hit a bit of a snag.

To get my free hobby project onto my friends' phones, the standard route was surprisingly expensive:

  • Google Play: $25 fee.
  • Apple App Store: $99 every single year.

For a big studio, that's just the cost of doing business. But for me? I just wanted to share something fun I made. Paying $100 just to let my friends play a memory game felt a bit excessive.

So, I looked for another way. And I found something really cool that I wanted to share with you all: Progressive Web Apps (PWA).

"Wait, it's just a website?"

I used to think that if a game wasn't on the App Store, it wasn't a "real" mobile game. I imagined clunky browser windows, address bars taking up screen space, and slow loading.

But it turns out, modern web tech has come a long way.

I learned that by turning Ditto! into a PWA, I could bypass the stores entirely but still give my friends that "native app" feeling.

  • They can install it: They just open the link, tap "Add to Home Screen," and boom! it's right there next to Instagram haha.

1. Tap the Share button

2. Tap 'Add to Home Screen'

3. Tap 'Add' to confirm

4. Enjoy the Native Experience

  • No Borders: Once they open it from the home screen, all the browser buttons disappear. It looks just like a regular app.
  • It works offline: Even if they lose signal, the game still works.

The best part? I didn't have to learn a new coding language like Swift or Kotlin. I built the whole thing using the web tools I already knew (Vite and JavaScript).

If you're using Vite, there's a plugin called vite-plugin-pwa that does most of the heavy lifting. You just need to add a little configuration that acts like an ID card for your app.

It looks something like this:

manifest: {
  name: 'Ditto!',
  display: 'standalone', // <--- The magic line that hides the browser UI
  theme_color: '#000000',
  icons: [ ... ]
}

That single line: display: 'standalone': was the game changer. It allowed me to send a link to my friend, have them add it to their home screen, and see their reaction when it opened up full-screen.

Why I loved this approach

Honest, the best part wasn't saving the money (though that was nice). It was the speed.

When I found a typo in the instructions, I just pushed the fix to GitHub. My friends got the update the next time they opened the app. No waiting 3 days for Apple to review my "typo fix."

It felt really freeing. It turned game development from a scary, expensive process into something casual and fun.

Give it a try!

If you have 5 minutes, you can try it out yourself.

👉 Play Ditto! here: https://zhnuksyh.github.io/ditto/

(Tip: If you're on your phone, try the "Share" -> "Add to Home Screen" trick. It’s pretty satisfying to see it turn into a real app icon!)

If you've been holding back on sharing your own projects because the App Store feels too intimidating, give PWAs a shot. It’s a really fun way to get your work out there.

articles.title: My Journey into AI Engineering: 4 Books Helping Me Bridge the Gap
articles.desc: Moving from tutorials to real-world AI engineering is a steep learning curve. Here are 4 books that helped me bridge the gap between coding and building useful solutions.
articles.fullContent:
I think we’ve all been there haha. You finish a machine learning tutorial, get that green checkmark, and feel like a genius. But then you start your first real internship (like I did recently at MIMOS), and suddenly, things get messy haha.

Real-world data isn't clean. Models hallucinate when you least expect it. And trying to deploy something that actual humans can use? That’s a whole different ball game compared to submitting an assignment on GitHub.

I’ve been trying to figure out how to move from just coding to actually building and creating scalable useful solutions that solve real problems. It’s been a steep learning curve, but I’ve found some resources that really helped the lightbulbs go on for me.

To be clear, I’m not a pro yet. I’m just another traveller on the same path as you, trying to figure this stuff out. I wanted to share the resources that are lighting the way for me, so we can move forward better together.

1. The LLM Engineer’s Handbook by Maxime Labonne & Paul Iusztin

Best For: Getting your hands dirty and building things from scratch.

If you’re on AI Twitter/X, you’ve probably seen Maxime’s amazing graphs. I picked this up because I wanted to understand what happens under the hood of the tools we use every day.

Why I Love It:
Most uni courses stop at "here is how to train a model." This book picks up right where they leave off. It walks you through the whole messy lifecycle of data prep, fine-tuning techniques (like QLoRA, which is super cool), and actually deploying on AWS.

My "Aha!" Moment:
I realized that if I want to build my own product one day, I can't just rely on expensive APIs forever. This book gave me the confidence to try hosting open-source models myself. It makes the scary infrastructure stuff feel manageable.

2. Building LLMs for Production by Louis-François Bouchard & Louie Peters

Best For: When you’re tired of your AI making things up haha.

You know that feeling when your chatbot works perfectly for you, but then breaks the second you show it to your boss? Yeah, that. This book is all about fixing that reliability gap.

Why I Love It:
Since I’m working on a mental health chatbot right now, reliability is huge for me. You can't have a therapist bot hallucinating! This book is a goldmine for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It basically teaches you how to give your AI a textbook so it doesn't just guess answers.

My "Aha!" Moment:
Prompt engineering is called engineering for a reason haha. This book taught me how to structure prompts systematically so the results are consistent, not just lucky.

3. Designing Machine Learning Systems by Chip Huyen

Best For: Seeing the big picture (and saving yourself headaches later).

This one is a classic for a reason. If the other books are about how to build, this one is about what to build and why.

Why I Love It:
Chip Huyen explains that a 99% accurate model is useless if it costs a fortune to run or takes ten seconds to reply. It helped me shift my focus from just chasing high accuracy scores to thinking about the user experience and business value.

My "Aha!" Moment:
It taught me to ask: "Do we even need ML for this?" sometimes the best engineering solution is the simplest one. It’s a great reality check for us students who want to use AI for everything.

4. AI Engineering by Chip Huyen

Best For: Understanding where our industry is going next.

Think of this as the modern update to the previous book. The industry is moving so fast, and the role of "Machine Learning Engineer" is evolving into "AI Engineer."

Why I Love It:
This feels like a peek into the future of our degree. It’s all about "Foundation Models" - using pre-trained giants to build products faster. It covers the new tech stack we’re all hearing about, like vector stores and LangChain.

My "Aha!" Moment:
We don't always have to reinvent the wheel! This book showed me the power of "composite AI systems", which chaining together existing powerful tools to build something cool and new.

Summary: What Should You Read?

If you're wondering where to start, here is how I break it down:

  • Want to build & deploy open-source models? Grab The LLM Engineer’s Handbook.
  • Struggling with hallucinations/RAG? Building LLMs for Production is your friend.
  • Want to design better systems overall? Designing Machine Learning Systems is essential.
  • Curious about the modern AI stack? Check out AI Engineering.

Grab the Books

To make it easier for you, I’ve uploaded all these e-books to a Google Drive folder. You can access them here: Download E-Books

Let's Learn Together

Transitioning from university to the industry is tough, and imposter syndrome is real. But books like these make the journey a lot less lonely.

Honestly, I’m still figuring all of this out myself. I’m sharing this list not because I have all the answers, but because I know how hard it can be to find the right map.

I’m learning something new every day, so I’d genuinely love to hear from you. Have you read any of these? Or do you have any other recommendations for a junior engineer like me?
